[ 01 ]

BriefBrief

AlphaPoint provides infrastructure for banks, exchanges, and fintech companies working with stablecoins and digital assets. Its marketing site needed to support a new visual direction, closer integration with its marketing tools, and more extensive animation.

Pony Studio handled the design. We handled the Webflow build and migration from WordPress.

[ 02 ]

SolutionSolution

Build the system behind the pages

The Figma designs became a Lumos-based Webflow system, with variables across theme modes to keep styles consistent as the site grows. The structure was set up so AlphaPoint's marketing team could assemble new pages from existing components rather than request builds.

Articles, resources, gated downloads, and team content moved from WordPress into Webflow CMS, with legacy URLs mapped to redirects so existing links and search rankings carried over to the new platform.

Make HubSpot part of the design

Embedded HubSpot forms were restyled across input states, error messages, and success behavior. The forms retained their tracking and workflows, including access to gated CMS content, while fitting the rest of the site.

Control when media loads and plays

The design relied on Lottie animation and video throughout. Video moved to external hosting, supported by a loading and playback system that delays assets and plays them when they enter view, keeping the media from competing with page content.

GSAP reveal animations completed the layouts, with timing matched to the brand so the motion reads as part of the design rather than an effect applied on top.

[ 03 ]

ResultResult

The site shipped on schedule with the CMS migrated, redirects in place, and HubSpot integrations live. AlphaPoint's marketing team gained a Webflow system it can extend, and Pony Studio's design survived production intact, from the theme variables down to the motion. The partnership model held throughout: design stayed with the agency, everything technical stayed with us.

[ 01 ]

BriefBrief

Jumpspeak helps over a million learners speak a new language through AI conversations. The app had moved to a new design system: dark, cinematic and built around real conversations. The landing page still looked like the old product, with a navy palette, stock imagery and a generic app-marketing layout.

That page is where paid traffic lands before the signup quiz, so it carries most of the acquisition load. Jumpspeak had already tested what made it convert. We needed to keep that logic and rebuild everything around it so the page felt like the app people were about to use.

[ 02 ]

SolutionSolution

A new visual language on a proven structure

Jumpspeak's existing homepage gave us the base: its content and structure were already working, so we kept them. The visual direction came from the app. We took key pieces of its design system, including the dark surfaces, accent blue and conversation UI, and built a page that looks and feels like the product people are about to open.

Show the product, not stock photos

The page demonstrates the product instead of describing it. The hero uses video persona cards speaking in the target language. Scenario chips, a live audio player and a face-to-face video conversation show each feature in action, and a tabbed carousel walks through real lessons for work, travel, dating and friends.

Rebuilt for conversion

On top of that structure, we tightened every step toward signup. Social proof sits in the hero subline. Every section closes with a CTA and the same risk reducer: 100 days risk-free, 23 languages. Reviews run in a two-row marquee with App Store and Google Play attribution, and the comparison table highlights Jumpspeak's column.

Heavy on motion, light on load

The page is full of video, animated UI and looping marquees, which is exactly what tends to make landing pages slow. Every animated asset is lazy loaded and optimized, so the motion appears as you scroll without slowing the first view.

A system under a legacy site

The existing Webflow site had no system behind it: no shared classes, no components, nothing to build on. Before any development, we integrated the Lumos framework properly across the project, giving the site a consistent structure for spacing, type and color.

Everything on the page is built from components the team can edit safely without breaking the layout. A library of Lumos base components lets them assemble new pages and sections from the same building blocks, so the site can keep growing at the same quality.

[ 03 ]

ResultResult

The acquisition page finally matches the product, and the site underneath it has a system it never had. What was a page-by-page legacy build is now componentized, themed, and built for motion, and Jumpspeak's team can create new pages from the same components, at the same quality, without starting from scratch.

[ 01 ]

BriefBrief

Navy Yard DC needed to help visitors find local businesses and explore the neighborhood. The site had to organize a large directory, surface businesses by category, and connect that content to an interactive map.

Planthouse supplied the design. We built the site in Webflow, including the CMS architecture, map filtering, and migration.

[ 02 ]

SolutionSolution

Organize content once

The directory spans more than 250 businesses and places, from restaurants and shops to parks, venues, and sports teams, organized across 30+ CMS collections. A shared tag system across categories including Shop & Dine, Sports & Entertainment, Parks & Plazas, and Health & Wellness lets a business appear in several relevant contexts without duplicate entries, so the BID team maintains each listing in one place.

Connect the directory to the map

A custom filtering layer linked Mapbox to the CMS tags. Selecting a category updated the map pins, letting visitors explore the same directory geographically, with the map and the listing pages always drawing from the same content. GSAP entrance sequences and scroll reveals added motion to key layouts.

Consolidate the migration

The move from Capitol Riverfront involved nearly 2,000 existing URLs, covering years of pages, events, and business listings. Rather than mapping each address individually, the URLs were consolidated into 133 redirect rules using Webflow's wildcard system, preserving the old site's routes with a set of rules small enough to maintain by hand.

[ 03 ]

ResultResult

The BID team gained a directory of 250+ businesses and places, an events calendar, and a map, all powered by the same content structure. New entries appear in the relevant categories and map views through a CMS update, with no developer involved, while the redirect setup carries visitors and search rankings from the previous site's URLs to the new one.

[ 01 ]

BriefBrief

Teal Health is the company behind the Teal Wand, an at-home sample collection device for cervical cancer screening. Its website needed to make the product easy to understand and the path to sign-up straightforward.

The existing site lacked a consistent system, making new pages harder to produce and maintain. The scope covered 30 redesigned pages, Webflow development, performance work, accessibility remediation, and continued support after launch.

[ 02 ]

SolutionSolution

Design and build from the same system

Typography, color, spacing, and components were defined in Figma and carried into Webflow on Lumos, with tokens shared across light, dark, and brand themes. The work was principal-led across design and development, with no handoffs. Responsive behavior, component reuse, and CMS structure were planned together, so decisions made in design survived into the build.

The resulting system gave the team reusable patterns for product pages, campaigns, and sign-up journeys, with the Teal Wand product page and its pricing and sign-up flow built from the same components as the rest of the site. Layout animations and interactions were tested across devices, including mobile Safari, where animation and video behavior tend to break first.

Improve loading around the existing tools

HubSpot, analytics, and consent management remained part of the site, so performance had to be won around them rather than by removing them. Script loading was reworked so page content takes priority and third-party tools wait until they are needed, and media loading was structured to protect layout stability.

The recorded mobile PageSpeed report shows a passed Core Web Vitals assessment based on real-user data: 1.5-second Largest Contentful Paint, 128 ms Interaction to Next Paint, and zero Cumulative Layout Shift. That zero means pages do not jump as they load, on a site that still runs marketing scripts on every page.

Address accessibility in the build

For a healthcare product, accessibility was treated as part of the build rather than a post-launch audit item. Work covered semantic structure, ARIA roles, accessible names on embedded HubSpot forms, and keyboard-operable interactions across the site's menus, accordions, and sliders.

Automated checks were paired with manual testing, including full keyboard navigation, and findings were addressed directly in the site's markup and behavior rather than logged for later. The same standards now apply to new pages added under the ongoing engagement.

[ 03 ]

ResultResult

Teal Health moved from a site assembled page by page to one system its team can grow, with mobile Core Web Vitals passing on real-user data and accessibility handled in the build rather than left for an audit. Design, development, and technical support stayed under one roof, and the work continues through an ongoing engagement, with new pages and campaigns built from the same foundation.

Start with the structure

Discovery with the client established the business goals, audience, and technical requirements. A new site structure and initial wireframes gave the design work a clear starting point.

We shaped the visual direction and reviewed the UI throughout production, keeping the layouts and brand expression aligned with the audience and the product.

Develop the illustrations and motion together

Animated illustrations were a central part of the homepage. We worked with the UI designer on illustration structure and layering, then with the motion designer on production and integration.

Custom playback controls managed the multiple Lottie animations on the page so they ran only when needed. GSAP and custom code handled the supporting interactions.

Build for ongoing use

The designs became responsive Webflow pages with reusable components and a maintainable structure, with us handling development directly so design intent survived the build. The client's team could extend the site using that foundation as new content was needed.

ResultResult

Tokenforge launched with a clearer presentation of a complex offering, a visual identity appropriate to institutional buyers, and animated illustrations that carry the explanation the old site couldn't. Strategy, art direction, and development ran through one lead, with specialist designers brought in where the work needed them, and the result is a Webflow system the team continues to use.
